title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page has two parts, both about elements of norm 1 in a quadratic extension L/K of number fields. In the 1965 'Galois theory of motives' context they are the arithmetic behind Weil numbers (Frobenius eigenvalues) lying in CM fields.

(1) Proposition. Let K be a number field and L/K quadratic with nontrivial automorphism σ. Let 𝔭 be a prime of K that splits in L as 𝔓𝔓' with 𝔓 ≠ 𝔓'. Then there is x ∈ L* with x·σ(x) = 1 and div(x) = 2h(𝔓 − 𝔓'), where h is the class number of L. The statement first says h(𝔓 − 𝔓'), but the proof gives 2h; Grothendieck adds 'div x = div z = 2 div y'.
- Proof: since h kills the class group, there is y with div y = h(𝔓 − 𝔓').
- Then div(σy) = h(𝔓' − 𝔓), so y·σy ∈ K* has divisor 0 and is a unit u.
- Put z = y² and x = z/u = y²/N_{L/K}(y).
- Then x·σx = (y·σy)²/u² = 1 and div x = 2h(𝔓 − 𝔓').

The margin sharpens this: the group of divisors of L of norm zero (combinations of 𝔓 − 𝔓' over split primes, plus multiples of inert or ramified primes) modulo divisors of elements with N_{L/K}x = 1 is a torsion group, killed by 2h. In modern terms, the norm-one torus T = ker(N: R_{L/K}G_m → G_m) has K-points whose divisors fill a finite-index subgroup of the norm-zero divisors.

(2) N.B. Let K be totally real and L a totally imaginary quadratic extension of K, i.e. a CM field, with complex conjugation written as a bar. Let p be a rational prime and 𝔭 a prime of K over p, and suppose 𝔭 does not split in L. The intended hypothesis is apparently that no prime of K above p splits. Let λ be an integer of L with λλ̄ = p^i, i.e. a Weil p^i-number of weight i in L.
- Then μ = λ²/p^i = λ²/N_{L/K}(λ) satisfies μμ̄ = 1.
- The non-split hypothesis makes the divisor of λ conjugation-invariant above p, so μ is a unit at every finite place.
- Since μμ̄ = 1 and conjugation is central in a CM field, |μ| = 1 at every archimedean place.
- By Kronecker's theorem μ is a root of unity, so λ = p^{i/2}·(root of unity).

Together, (1) and (2) form the dichotomy behind the structure of Weil numbers in CM fields. Nontrivial norm-one elements with prescribed divisor 𝔓 − 𝔓' come only from split primes. Over non-split primes a Weil number is p^{i/2} times a root of unity, the 'supersingular' case.
errors: The statement claims divisor h(𝔓−𝔓'), but the construction gives 2h(𝔓−𝔓'); Grothendieck corrects this in the interlinear note.
The detour via z = y² and u is unnecessary: x = y/σy has norm 1 and divisor 2h(𝔓−𝔓') directly.

In the N.B., concluding that μ is a unit needs every prime of K above p to be non-split in L, not just one 𝔭. Only if all such primes are non-split is μ a unit everywhere, and the CM hypothesis is what gives |μ| = 1 archimedeanly. The hypotheses are written only partly legibly.
μ having absolute value 1 is a root of unity only by Kronecker's theorem, which is used implicitly. 'u voisine de l'unité' should almost certainly read 'u racine de l'unité'.

ideas.what: Elements of norm 1 in a quadratic extension with prescribed divisor supported on split primes, via the class number (y/σy or y²/Ny).
ideas.modern_name: K-points of the norm-one torus and their divisors; ingredient in the structure of Weil-number groups
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (Hilbert 90 and class group finiteness); used systematically by Honda, Tate and Serre around 1967-70

ideas.what: The group of norm-zero divisors modulo divisors of norm-one elements is torsion.
ideas.modern_name: finiteness/torsion in the divisor map of the norm-one torus

ideas.what: A Weil p^i-number in a CM field where p does not split is p^{i/2} times a root of unity.
ideas.modern_name: supersingular Weil numbers; part of Honda–Tate theory and Milne's Weil-number torus
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tate (1966-68), Honda (1968), Manin; later Milne/Langlands–Rapoport for the Weil-number group

missed.claim: Grothendieck was computing the arithmetic of Weil numbers in CM fields (split vs non-split primes, norm-one elements with prescribed divisors) in the motivic-Galois notes. This is evidence he was thinking about the Frobenius side of motives over finite fields, i.e. the Weil-number torus later formalised by Langlands–Rapoport and Milne. The mathematics itself is elementary and well known.
missed.quote: Donc λ = p^{i/2}u, u [racine] de l'unité !
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of historical interest only: it documents early engagement with what became the Weil-number group / Taniyama-type groups, contemporaneous with Tate's work. It adds no new result.

deep.surprise_reason: The results are elementary and classical. The only interest is historical: they show Grothendieck working on the Weil-number arithmetic underlying motives over finite fields in 1965.
transcription_corrections: 'u voisine de l'unité' at the end is almost certainly 'u racine de l'unité'; similarly earlier occurrences of 'voisine de l'unité' likely read 'racine de l'unité'.
Interlinear: 'où h ∈ ℕ*' and later 'si h est l'ordre du groupe des classes (de div.) de L'.
The line '= 2h(𝔭−𝔭')' completes 'on aura div x = 2h(𝔓−𝔓')'.
N.B. hypothesis: 'Soit K totalement réel, et L ext. quadratique de K, totalement imaginaire'. The hypothesis is that 𝔭 is the only prime of L above 𝔭 (non-split), not that it splits.
The previous and next pages are typescript pages of Steinberg's 'Regular elements of semisimple algebraic groups' (1965), unrelated to this page.
